The result of an inversion is

Think of it this way: if you measure a total weight of 1 kg, the box could contain
one 1 kg object, or ten 100 g objects, or a thousand 1 g objects. The surface
measurement alone cannot tell you which.
To make the result more trustworthy, geophysicists use
— a mathematical way of adding prior knowledge or preferences to guide the solution. Common choices include:
: prefer models where neighbouring cells are similar (avoids unrealistic sharp jumps)
: account for the fact that deeper cells are less well constrained by surface data
: anchor the inversion to a known starting point (e.g. from a borehole)
✅ What makes a good inversion result?

children.label: ✅ What makes a good inversion result?

children.value: A result is considered reliable when:
— the forward model of the result closely reproduces the measured signal
— small changes in starting conditions do not produce wildly different images
with independent information (borehole logs, soil cores, known geology)
confirms that the features of interest are actually resolved by the data, not artefacts of the algorithm

In post-fire studies, this last point deserves special attention. Fire-induced changes in soil properties can be subtle, localised, and overprinted by natural variability. A feature visible in a geophysical image is only meaningful if it can be shown — through sensitivity tests or ground-truth sampling — that the data were actually capable of resolving it.
